deep.reconstruction:
Three short notes, dated August 1796 (Gauss was 19). Two of them sit next to the 17-gon period of the Tagebuch.

(A) 'Demonstratio elementaris propositionis de productis e cosinibus' (Aug. 21, 1796).
1. The double-angle formula gives sin(pi/13)·cos(pi/13) = (1/2)·sin(2pi/13).
2. Multiplying again by cos(2pi/13) gives (1/2)·sin(2pi/13)·cos(2pi/13) = (1/4)·sin(4pi/13), 'and so on'.
3. By induction (my explicit statement): sin(pi/13) · prod_{k=0}^{n-1} cos(2^k·pi/13) = 2^{-n}·sin(2^n·pi/13).
4. If at last sin(2^n·pi/13) = ±sin(pi/13), then prod_{k=0}^{n-1} cos(2^k·pi/13) = ±1/2^n.
5. Gauss does not say when this happens. The condition is 2^n ≡ ±1 (mod 13). Since 2 is a primitive root mod 13, the first case is n = 6, because 2^6 = 64 = 5·13 − 1.
6. Then sin(64pi/13) = sin(5pi − pi/13) = +sin(pi/13). So cos(pi/13)·cos(2pi/13)·cos(4pi/13)·cos(8pi/13)·cos(16pi/13)·cos(32pi/13) = 1/64.
7. Sign check (mine): only the factors with 8pi/13 and 16pi/13 are negative, so the product is positive.
8. 'In the same way' the product cos(m·pi/13)·cos(2m·pi/13)···cos(2^{n-1}m·pi/13) gives the same product. Indeed, for 13 ∤ m the same telescoping gives sin(64m·pi/13)/(64·sin(m·pi/13)) = −(−1)^m/64. That is +1/64 for odd m and −1/64 for even m, so it agrees with Gauss's ± formulation.
9. Gauss remarks that these facts also follow 'without any calculation, by mere inspection of the polygon', i.e. the regular 13-gon (equivalently 26-gon).

(B) Geometric proof (same day, 'Eodem').
- Claim: sum_{k=0}^{n-1} cos(2pi·k/n) = 0.
- Place the regular n-gon so that one side is horizontal, as in the sketch. The sides, taken in order, are vectors of equal length with directions 2pi·k/n. Their horizontal projections (the dashed lines in the figure) are proportional to cos(2pi·k/n).
- Because the polygon closes, these projections sum to zero (n ≥ 2).

(C) Summation of periodic divergent series (Aug. 28, 1796).
1. Let the series repeat a period a, b, c, …, l of length n with a + b + … + l = 0, e.g. 1 − 1 + 1 − 1 …
2. Multiply the k-th term by x^k. The series becomes recurrent with sum (a + b·x + c·x^2 + … + l·x^{n-1})/(1 − x^n).
3. At x = 1 this is 0/0. By 'the known rules' (L'Hôpital) the value is −(b + 2c + … + (n−1)·l)/n = −(1/n)·sum_k k·a_k.
4. Implicit check (mine): this equals the mean of the partial sums over one period, (1/n)·sum_{j=0}^{n-1} s_j = sum_k a_k − (1/n)·sum_k k·a_k = −(1/n)·sum_k k·a_k.
5. That mean is the value Daniel Bernoulli had obtained by a 'metaphysical principle, namely of sufficient reason' (equal likelihood of stopping at any point of the period). Examples: 1 − 1 + 1 − … = 1/2 and 1 + 0 − 1 + 1 + 0 − 1 … = 2/3.
6. Gauss asserts the two values coincide, and they do.
errors: In the condition 'sin(2^n pi/13) = ±sin 1/13' the factor pi is missing on the right-hand side; it should read sin(pi/13). This is a slip of the pen.
The general-m statement ('dare idem productum') holds only up to sign and requires 13 ∤ m. The product is +1/64 for odd m and −1/64 for even m (n = 6). Gauss's ± covers this, but 'idem' is loose.
The stopping index n is not specified. It must satisfy 2^n ≡ ±1 (mod 13); the minimal case is n = 6.
No substantive errors in parts B and C. The L'Hôpital evaluation and its agreement with Bernoulli's mean value are correct.

results.what: Product prod_{k=0}^{5} cos(2^k·pi/13) = 1/64 via repeated double-angle telescoping, and its generalization to cos(2^k·m·pi/13).
results.modern_name: Telescoping product cos x·cos 2x···cos 2^{n-1}x = sin(2^n x)/(2^n sin x), combined with 2 being a primitive root mod 13 (Gauss-period-style product)
results.usually_credited_to: Telescoping identity: classical (Viète/Euler era). Application to Gauss periods: Gauss's cyclotomy (Disquisitiones, 1801).

results.what: Sum of cos(2pi·k/n) over k = 0..n−1 is 0, proved by projecting the sides of a regular polygon.
results.modern_name: Vanishing sum of the n-th roots of unity (real part), via closed-polygon vector sum
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euler/de Moivre era); the geometric proof is folklore

results.what: Abel-type summation of periodic series with zero period sum, (a + bx + … )/(1 − x^n) as x → 1 via L'Hôpital. The result equals Daniel Bernoulli's mean-of-partial-sums value.
results.modern_name: Abel summation of periodic series; agreement with Cesàro (C,1) mean
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (power-series method, 1750s); Daniel Bernoulli (1771, probabilistic argument); Lagrange (1799, on Callet's objection)

deep.surprise_reason: These are student exercises from the period of the 17-gon discovery. The cosine product is an instance of Gauss periods and fits his known cyclotomy work. The divergent-series remark reproduces known Euler/Bernoulli/Lagrange material. The page is of biographical interest only, not a priority claim.

Sum of cos(2pi·k/n) over a full period is 0 (n = 7)
Periodic series 1 + 0 − 1 + 1 + 0 − 1 … has Abel sum 2/3, Daniel Bernoulli's value

transcription_corrections: 'tenentium' is written 'tenenti' with the ending '-um' carried to the next line.
In 'sin 2^n pi/13 = ± sin 1/13' the manuscript indeed omits pi on the right; this is Gauss's slip, not a transcription error.
'huius seriei [struck-out word] quae est recurrens': the deleted word is illegible and possibly the start of 'summa'.
'D. D. Bern.' = Daniel Bernoulli. 'D. D.' is likely 'Dominus Doctor' (an honorific), not a doubled initial.
